The First Battle of Bull Run. Also called the First Battle of Manassas, fought on July twenty-first, eighteen sixty-one near Manassas, Virginia. It was the first major military engagement of the American Civil War. Though it ended in Confederate victory, it shattered Northern hopes for a swift, decisive victory and signaled that the war would be prolonged and costly.

The battle was fought on July twenty-first, eighteen sixty-one, less than three months after the firing on Fort Sumter, representing the Union's first major offensive operation of the war. Northern commanders, confident of victory and under political pressure to act, marched into Virginia expecting to overwhelm Confederate forces and recapture the strategic interior quickly. President Lincoln believed a swift victory would demoralize the South and end the rebellion, while Northern newspapers proclaimed a picnic-like atmosphere and easy triumph. Confederate forces, led by P.G.T. Beauregard and reinforced by Joseph Johnston's army from the Shenandoah Valley, were well-positioned to defend the ground and staged an effective defense. Thomas Jackson's unflinching stand on Henry House Hill earned him the nickname Stonewall, becoming one of the war's great myths and establishing him as a military legend. Union forces initially seemed to be winning in the morning, flanking the Confederate left flank, but Confederate reinforcements arrived at the critical moment via the Manassas Gap Railroad. Union forces, including many civilian observers who brought picnic baskets expecting an easy spectacle, were routed and retreated chaotically back toward Washington, shocking the North with the reality of warfare. Casualties were modest by later standards—approximately six hundred killed from both sides—but striking to a nation unprepared for sustained warfare and the scale of modern combat. The battle demonstrated that the Confederacy was capable of serious military resistance and killed any illusion of a ninety-day war, forcing the North to prepare for prolonged conflict. The First Battle of Bull Run connects to the American Civil War as the opening engagement of the conflict; Fort Sumter as the triggering event that preceded Bull Run by months; Thomas Jackson who earned Stonewall at this battle for his steadfast defense; the Battle of Antietam as a later and far bloodier engagement in the same region; P.G.T. Beauregard as Confederate commander at Bull Run; George McClellan as Union general who would take command afterward; and the Battle of Gettysburg as another pivotal battle that would occur two years later.
